verdicts.flaw_description: In two of the four plots the outcome is dated before the intervention: the tomato was 'fed 3 August' but measured 'by 20 June', and the oak was 'fed 2 May' but measured 'by 19 April', while the other two plots (8 January to 26 February, 7 October to 24 November) run forward. Half the cases therefore record the height gain before the fertilizer was applied.

A named alternative cause reaches every section: 'The central syllabus set coursework at a third of the final grade, up from a quarter, and every section was marked to that central syllabus.' Raising coursework from 25 to 33 percent of the final grade between the earlier year and this one would by itself push completion up in all four sections, so the 6 to 11 point rise cannot be attributed to the lab kit.

The timings cover a narrower population than the claim: 'Timings cover the runs that stayed on the issued route, and about a sixth of each depot's runs left the issued route.' Roughly one run in six is dropped from the average, and those deviating runs are exactly the ones likely to be slow, so the 5 to 9 minute improvement is measured only on a self-selected compliant subset rather than on delivery runs generally.

The absence figures cover a narrower group than the cohorts the claim is about: 'Absence figures cover the pupils on the revised timetable throughout, and about a fifth of each cohort spent weeks on the old timetable.' A fifth of each cohort is excluded from the count, and pupils who were off the revised timetable for weeks plausibly include the poorest attenders, so the 4 to 7 percent drop reflects a filtered subset rather than the cohort.
